A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InfoBridge, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite appendix renumbering, relocations, and additions.

before.justification: v3 reports original MI-estimation experiments in Section 5, entropy-estimation results in Appendix C.3, and ablations in Appendix D.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds training-duration, training-set-size, sampling-strategy, and network-sharing experiments in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The drift-difference estimator, shared conditional network, and default algorithms are retained. Section 4.2 and Appendix C.4 introduce optional derangement permutations and fresh marginal draws for constructing independent training pairs, providing limited procedural variants.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same low-dimensional distributions, synthetic Gaussian/rectangle images, protein embeddings, high-MI distributions, and exponential/uniform entropy tasks. The new studies vary configurations within existing coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain their baseline memberships, including MINDE variants, NVF/JVF, AE-WKL, and fDIME variants. SMILE is newly named in related work but is not evaluated. Added studies reuse existing baselines or examine InfoBridge variants.

E3.justification: New protocols vary training duration, sampling strategy, network sharing, and training-set size, with smaller networks accompanying the 5k/10k datasets. Reported settings also change: v4 specifies protein batch size 128 and high-MI training for 200 epochs with batch size 128, whereas v3 inherited batch size 512 and, for high MI, 100k steps. v4 retains conflicting appendix references to the earlier recipe; reruns are not established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained volatility, network-width, and Monte Carlo sample-count analyses, v4 adds training-dynamics analysis, reduced-training-data comparisons, independent-pair sampling ablations, and a direct one-network versus two-network comparison (Tables 7–10). These substantially expand validation of practical design choices.

E5.justification: Existing seed counts, standard deviations, and 99% confidence-interval reporting are retained. Appendix D.1 newly documents a standard-deviation calculation, but its printed formula omits squared deviations and has inconsistent indexing. This changes the statistical documentation without establishing recomputation or additional runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark accuracy tables remain numerically unchanged. Substantial new results cover training dynamics, smaller datasets, sampling variants, network sharing, and runtimes. For example, v4 Table 9 reports MAE 12.24 for ordinary permutation, 10.51 for derangement, and 10.62 for fresh draws; these are newly reported variant comparisons.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 replaces a generic external regularity reference with explicit finite-MI and first-moment requirements. New Appendix A.1 supplies h-function regularity lemmas, a conditional SDE representation, and the drift-identity derivation. Appendix A.2 expands the KL proof with a truncated-time argument and limiting step, substantially extending the mathematical treatment.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and discussion retain the same central claims: an unbiased theoretical MI estimator based on bridge matching, a practical InfoBridge algorithm, and strong performance on challenging benchmarks. The added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds an epsilon bias–variance interpretation and sampling-correlation caveat, and replaces the asserted bias-correlation explanation for network sharing with an empirical comparison. It removes v3's general small-training-set limitation and introduces robustness interpretations, while retaining the heavy-tail applicability boundary.

D1.justification: v4 adds an estimator-code access link, discloses time sampling below 0.999, and provides additional parameter counts, timings, and hardware information. Conversely, the autoencoder architecture in v3 Table 8 disappears from v4 Table 12 despite retention of AE-WKL experiments. These revise an already detailed implementation appendix.

R1.justification: v4 adds recent bridge-model references and theoretical sources including Doob (1957) and Léonard (2012, 2013), while removing Yoon et al. (2023) and the associated long-tailed-diffusion suggestion. The principal positioning against MINDE and other estimator families remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact. v4 moves the diffusion-KL background into Section 4.1, moves and shortens limitations into Section 7, corrects cross-references and terminology, expands explanations, and updates affiliations and publication headers.

P2.justification: v4 adds displays covering convergence, training-data size, sampling variants, network sharing, and runtime comparisons (Tables 7–10, 13, 15, and 20). Existing plots are retained but relocated, including the exchanged numbering of protein and high-MI figures. The architecture table loses its autoencoder block, and several captions are revised.

improvement.justification: The previously asserted advantage of sharing a network gains direct experimental support in Table 10, while other new ablations and explicit theoretical assumptions improve assessability. These benefits are tempered by conflicting training-budget descriptions, removal of the AE-WKL architecture, and errors in the new standard-deviation formula and Equation 17, which equates unrestricted process KL with a truncated-time integral. The net gain is useful but limited.
